title: Which lockers are still open after all one hundred people pass?
description: The video answers the queen's puzzle by linking an open locker to an odd number of factors, and finds which lockers up to one hundred have that. Keeko doubts that the odd numbered lockers are the ones that stay open.
teaching_notes: One idea: a locker ends open only if its number has an odd number of factors, and that happens only for numbers made by multiplying a number by itself. Watch for students who think the odd numbered lockers stay open.

source: Which lockers remain open after all 100 people pass?
video_script.why: The child connects an open locker with an odd number of factors, and sees that these lockers are the square numbers up to one hundred.
video_script.substitution: Say a locker ends open when its factor count is odd, then find the numbers that pair a factor with itself.
video_script.anchor: the row of one hundred lockers of {{NAME_1}}
video_script.wrong_answer: the odd numbered lockers stay open
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko links open with odd and says the odd numbered lockers stay open. It is the number of factors that has to be odd, and locker three has two factors, so it ends closed.
video_script.payoff_line: The squares up to one hundred stay open

final_answer.spoken: the squares up to one hundred stay open

names.{{NAME_1}}: the queen of Khoisnam whose will hides the treasure in one of 100 lockers

never_show: the exercise answer: the first five lockers touched exactly twice are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11
maths_rules: all lockers start closed; an odd number of toggles leaves a locker open, an even number leaves it closed
the number of toggles of a locker equals the number of its factors
factors pair up, so the count is odd only when a pair repeats the same number: k × k
the slip: locker 3 has the factors 1 and 3, so 2 toggles, and it ends closed; locker 4 has 1, 2, 4, so 3 toggles, and it ends open
video_script.design: One idea: open means an odd count of factors, which means a number times itself. Wrong idea: odd lockers stay open. The row of lockers stays in the anchor band.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; a row of one hundred closed lockers in the anchor band with a hundred small people walking by; an empty box for the open lockers

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.row: the row of closed lockers appears
marks.walk: the people walk past the row
marks.ask: an empty box for the open lockers appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='row'/>{{NAME_1}} left one hundred lockers, all closed.
<bookmark mark='walk'/>One hundred people pass by, and each toggles some of the lockers.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which lockers remain open after all one hundred people have passed?

beats.on_screen: the question holds still and the empty box glows

marks.stop: the empty box glows in the accent colour

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: one locker on the stage: the door goes closed, open, closed, open as flips are counted

marks.one: the door swings open after the first flip
marks.two: the door swings shut after the second flip
marks.more: the door keeps swinging with each flip, open after an odd flip and closed after an even flip

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Every locker starts closed, so one flip leaves it open.
<bookmark mark='two'/>A second flip shuts it again.
<bookmark mark='more'/>An odd number of flips leaves it open, and an even number leaves it closed.

beats.on_screen: Given: 100 lockers, all closed; person k toggles every k-th locker
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, one hundred lockers start closed, and one hundred people toggle them in turn.

beats.on_screen: To find: the lockers that are open at the end

marks.find: the thing to find is written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the lockers that stay open at the end.

beats.on_screen: open locker: odd number of toggles = odd number of factors

marks.odd: the words odd number of toggles are written
marks.link: an arrow links toggles to factors

narration: <bookmark mark='odd'/>Step one, a locker ends open only if it is flipped an odd number of times.
<bookmark mark='link'/>Each person who flips a locker is a factor of its number. We need an odd number of factors.

beats.on_screen: factors in pairs: an odd count needs a pair like k × k

marks.pairs: pairs of factors are joined by arcs
marks.same: one pair has the same number twice and its arc closes into a loop

narration: <bookmark mark='pairs'/>Step two, factors come in pairs, so the count is usually even.
<bookmark mark='same'/>It is odd only when one pair is a number with itself, like six times six.

marks.def: the words square number appear beside k × k
marks.rows: the ten products from one times one to ten times ten appear one after another

narration: <bookmark mark='def'/>Step three, a square number means a number multiplied by itself.
<bookmark mark='rows'/>Go from one times one up to ten times ten, since ten times ten is one hundred.

marks.list: the ten locker numbers light up one after another

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The squares up to one hundred stay open.
<bookmark mark='list'/>They are lockers one, four, nine, sixteen and twenty five.
Then thirty six, forty nine, sixty four, eighty one and one hundred.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: odd lockers open; locker 3 has factors 1, 3 and ends closed; locker 4 has 1, 2, 4 and ends open

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble says odd lockers open
marks.three: locker three is flipped twice and ends closed
marks.four: locker four is flipped three times and ends open

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the odd numbered lockers stay open, because open goes with odd.
<bookmark mark='three'/>But locker three has only two factors, one and three, so it ends closed.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Locker four is even, yet it has three factors, one, two and four. It ends open.
